title: Model Context Protocol, explained
description: Understand hosts, clients, servers, and the capabilities they exchange.
objectives: Map host, client, and server responsibilities
explanation: Model Context Protocol defines a common way for AI applications to connect with external capabilities. A host application manages the user experience and connections. A client participates in the protocol connection to a server. A server exposes capabilities such as tools or contextual data. MCP is an integration protocol, not a model and not a guarantee of trustworthy content.

Tools represent callable operations; resources expose contextual data; prompts offer reusable interaction templates. Keep these responsibilities distinct when designing a server. A document source may provide read-only resources, while a ticketing integration may expose a tool to create a ticket.

MCP has two layers. The data layer uses JSON-RPC 2.0 messages for discovery and primitives such as tools/list and tools/call. The transport layer carries those messages: stdio for a local server process, or Streamable HTTP for remote servers, where MCP recommends OAuth to obtain tokens. A host creates one client per server connection.

Protocol details change between versions. In version 2026-07-28, each request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in a _meta field, and servers answer a server/discover request. Read the specification for the version you target. Regardless of transport, the host must preserve user control and application authorization. Discovering a tool does not imply permission to execute it.

terms.definition: The AI application managing user interaction and connections.
The protocol participant connecting to a server.
The channel carrying MCP messages, such as stdio or Streamable HTTP.

example: In a policy assistant, the host connects through an MCP client to a policy server. The server advertises a search tool and policy resources. The host checks user permissions and presents source material; it does not treat a retrieved policy as an instruction to execute another tool.

mistakes: Treating MCP as a replacement for authorization.
Assuming every server supports every capability.
Copying transport examples without checking their protocol version.
exercise: Design an inventory server with one read-only tool, one resource, and one prompt template. State what identity and permission checks each needs.

questions.question: Is MCP itself a language model?
questions.answer: No. It is a protocol for connecting AI applications to external capabilities and context.
questions.distractor: Yes, it is a model that trains on connected databases.

questions.question: What is the host responsible for?
questions.answer: The host manages the application experience and connections, including how users control access and actions.
questions.distractor: The host must blindly execute every discovered tool.

questions.question: Does discovering a ticket-creation tool authorize its use?
questions.answer: No. The application still needs to check identity, permissions, arguments, and any required approval.
questions.distractor: Yes, discovery grants all users execution rights.

questions.question: How do resources differ from tools?
questions.answer: Resources expose contextual data; tools expose callable operations. The application should preserve that distinction.

questions.question: Why check the protocol version before using a transport example?
questions.answer: Connection and transport requirements evolve; an example for another version may be incompatible with your deployment.
